title: Understanding the 2026 US midterms
lede: Who was elected, how the US system works, and what a Democratic Congress can and cannot change at home and abroad. Based on projections from 4 to 6 November 2026; some counts are still firming.

cells: Democrats win control, with at least 33 pickups
Democrats win control with at least 54 seats including independents who caucus with them; seven flips: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina, Texas

table.note: Alaska and Mississippi Senate races were uncalled at the time of the sources. Outlets report different final House counts while dozens of races are uncounted, so treat exact numbers as provisional.

elects: All 435 members of the House of Representatives, for two-year terms, and 35 of the 100 senators, for six-year terms. Two of the Senate races were special elections to fill vacancies. Voters in 36 states also chose governors.
It is called a midterm because it falls halfway through the president's four-year term. The president, Donald Trump, was not on the ballot, but the vote worked as a verdict on his second term so far.

system.oneline: Each seat is won by whoever gets the most votes in its district or state. Parties win control by winning enough seats.

steps.p: Each district elects one member, and the winner is the candidate with the most votes. Control needs 218 seats. District lines are redrawn by states, which is why maps and populations matter.
Each state has two senators regardless of size, one third of seats up every two years. A party needs 51 seats, or 50 plus the vice president's tie-breaking vote.
Governors are chosen statewide, with the most votes winning in nearly every state.
County maps show where land and votes sit, not where people live. These pages redraw each race by population so a county of ten voters is not the same size as one with a million.

home: Divided government is back. Democrats can block administration priorities, run investigations and use the power of the purse, since spending bills start in the House. Through the Senate they decide which presidential nominees are confirmed.

home.p: Donald Trump can keep acting through executive action and can veto legislation. Democrats do not have a veto-proof two-thirds majority, so they cannot override him alone.
Analysts read the result partly as a referendum on affordability and on perceived political corruption, and on a Republican message that did not land.

world.p: Tariffs rest on authority Congress already delegated to the president, so a change in who controls Congress does not by itself change them. Democrats can hold hearings, press companies on refunds, and push bills to limit that authority, but a veto would stand.

Democrats are generally more supportive of Ukraine and NATO and can bring aid to a vote. But Trump may push for a war-ending deal on terms unfavourable to Ukraine, and a better US relationship with Europe is not guaranteed. Congress has already required at least 76,000 US troops in Europe.
The new Congress can hold hearings on the Iran war, use funding to restrict operations and limit military aid. Binding limits face the veto.
The House controls the purse and can investigate the dissolution of USAID. Expect oversight of US strikes on suspected drug boats off South America, rather than quick legislation.

Ukrainian outlets called it a possible boost. Allies hoped for a check on Trump but analysts stressed that the president keeps control of foreign policy, and the Kremlin was reported to be optimistic.

p: Republicans would have kept unified control: no hearings with subpoena power, an easier path for nominees and spending bills, and fewer constraints on tariffs, Iran policy and aid cuts.

Allies would have read it as a mandate for the current direction, with less hope of a congressional counterweight on Ukraine and NATO. The balance of power in Washington and the signal to the world are what changed.
